citation: Liu et al. (2024), “Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts”
explanation: Liu et al. (2024), “Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts” Liu et al. study how language models use long inputs on multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval, varying the position of the information needed to answer. They find a pronounced positional effect: performance is often strongest when relevant information appears near the beginning or end of the context and drops substantially when it is placed in the middle, even for models explicitly designed to accept long contexts. Limitation: The study’s limitation is that it uses two controlled information-identification tasks and the model generation available at the time, so it does not establish the same curve for every form of long-context reasoning, agent trace, modality, or current frontier model.

explanation: Sun et al. (2021), “Do Long-Range Language Models Actually Use Long-Range Context?” Sun et al. perform a fine-grained analysis of two long-range Transformer language models that accept sequences up to 8K tokens, asking whether context beyond the recent local window improves prediction. explanation: Oakhill, Johnson-Laird & Garnham (1989), “Believability and Syllogistic Reasoning” This paper tests belief bias in syllogistic reasoning by examining whether believability affects premise interpretation, the examination of alternative representations, or the final filtering of candidate conclusions. Across three experiments involving both conclusion generation and conclusion evaluation, participants were influenced by beliefs at the alternative-model and conclusion-filtering stages, not only during initial premise interpretation. Limitation: The limitation is that the evidence concerns human subjects and controlled syllogistic materials, so it does not directly quantify LLM reasoning or distinguish all modern failure modes such as parsing and format errors.

citation: Xu, Shi, and Choi (2023/ICLR 2024), “RECOMP: Improving Retrieval-Augmented LMs with Compression and Selective Augmentation”
explanation: RECOMP: Improving Retrieval-Augmented LMs with Compression and Selective Augmentation Xu, Shi, and Choi (ICLR 2024) introduce RECOMP, a retrieval-context compressor trained with downstream language-model performance as the objective, with both extractive and abstractive variants and the ability to return an empty string when retrieved evidence is not useful. The method improves retrieval-augmented generation by reducing distractors and selectively augmenting the generator with evidence that helps answer the task, demonstrating that compression can be learned as an end-task utility decision rather than as generic summarization. citation: (Findings of ACL 2024), “Effective In-Context Example Selection through Data Compression”
explanation: Effective In-Context Example Selection through Data Compression Sun et al. (Findings ACL 2024) frame few-shot example selection as data compression and introduce a two-stage method: BM25 first recalls examples relevant to the query, then an influence-aware reranking stage uses a meta-gradient/Fisher approximation to select examples that preserve useful information from the broader training set. Across five real-world datasets and four GPT-2 model sizes, the method reports an average improvement of 5.90% and consistently outperforms its BM25 comparison under three- and four-example settings. Limitation: Its limitation is that it compresses the example set rather than the internal content of each example, and the selection signal is relevance plus parameter influence rather than argument roles, logical form, or proof dependency.

citation: Pan et al. (2024), “LLMLingua-2: Data Distillation for Efficient and Faithful Task-Agnostic Prompt Compression”
explanation: LLMLingua-2: Data Distillation for Efficient and Faithful Task-Agnostic Prompt Compression Pan et al. (Findings ACL 2024) recast prompt compression as token classification: an LLM generates compression supervision, and a smaller bidirectional encoder is distilled to decide which tokens to retain or remove using full contextual information. The resulting compressor is faster and more faithful than repeatedly invoking a large autoregressive model, and the paper reports strong task-agnostic compression performance across multiple benchmarks. Limitation: The central limitation is representational: the classifier predicts token retention labels rather than identifying argument components, logical relations, proof dependencies, or source-grounded propositions, so it may retain a useful lexical surface while discarding a low-frequency but globally essential premise.

citation: Li, Dong, Lin, and Guerin (2023), “Compressing Context to Enhance Inference Efficiency of Large Language Models (Selective Context)”
explanation: Compressing Context to Enhance Inference Efficiency of Large Language Models (Selective Context) Li et al. (EMNLP 2023) present Selective Context, a model-agnostic method that removes redundant lexical units—tokens, phrases, or sentences—using surprisal and information-based criteria, then evaluates the shortened context on long documents, news, and conversations. The paper provides a simple and broadly applicable baseline for reducing input length while retaining generation quality and faithfulness, making explicit that local information content can guide inference-time pruning without retraining the target model. Limitation: Its limitation is the mismatch between local redundancy and global reasoning value: a premise may be locally predictable or low-surprisal yet indispensable to a conclusion, and the method does not recover argument roles or dependencies.

citation: Chevalier, Wettig, Ajith, and Chen (2023), “Adapting Language Models to Compress Contexts (AutoCompressors)”
explanation: Adapting Language Models to Compress Contexts (AutoCompressors) Chevalier et al. (EMNLP 2023) train language models to convert long text segments into compact continuous summary vectors or soft prompts, recursively passing compressed memory forward so later computation can condition on earlier content without rereading the full text. The paper demonstrates that latent compressed context can support long-context language modeling, compressed demonstrations, retrieval-augmented use, and passage reranking, showing that raw text is not always necessary at inference time. Limitation: Its key limitation is opacity: the latent vectors have no directly inspectable argument units, logical relations, or span-level provenance, and compression is representational rather than an explicit extract-then-select pipeline.

explanation: In-context Autoencoder for Context Compression in a Large Language Model (ICAE) Ge et al. (ICLR 2024) introduce ICAE, a lightweight compressor that maps long contexts into compact memory slots consumed directly by a base LLM, using autoencoding/language-modeling pretraining followed by instruction tuning. The method reports substantial reductions in context length, latency, and GPU-memory use while retaining useful task behavior, establishing a practical latent-memory route that does not require changing the full target model. Limitation: Its limitation is that the memory slots are opaque and there is no explicit extraction of claims, premises, warrants, proof steps, or logical relations, nor a selective retention stage that identifies which source spans support the downstream answer.

citation: Mu et al. (2023), “Learning to Compress Prompts with Gist Tokens”
explanation: Learning to Compress Prompts with Gist Tokens Mu et al. (NeurIPS 2023) propose gist tokens, a small set of learned tokens into which a model encodes prompts, instructions, or demonstrations so that the compressed representation can be reused in subsequent generation. Experiments with decoder-only and encoder-decoder models show large prompt-length reductions while preserving task behavior, making gist tokens a reusable primitive for few-shot examples and repeated instructions. Limitation: The limitation is that the representation is learned end to end and is not required to expose or preserve explicit argument components, logical relations, negation, numerical qualifiers, or provenance links to the original prompt.

citation: Kim, Yeom, Yun, and Song (2023/ICLR 2024), “Compressed Context Memory for Online Language Model Interaction”
explanation: Compressed Context Memory for Online Language Model Interaction Kim et al. (ICLR 2024) propose a recurrent key/value-memory compressor for online interaction, continually folding accumulated Transformer attention keys and values into a compact memory using a lightweight conditional LoRA inserted into the forward pass, without fine-tuning all model weights. The method is trained through a parallelized formulation of recursive compression and performs at the level of a full-context model with approximately 5× smaller context memory; it also supports streaming interaction with unbounded context and outperforms a sliding-window baseline. Limitation: Its limitation is that compression occurs inside model state rather than through an inspectable textual or symbolic representation, so users cannot audit which propositions were retained or recover source-span provenance.
